opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it was a kind of stubbornness that came from being young, but also from a very gut-level feeling. When I was an undergrad, I had already gotten hooked on vision. There was something about images that just felt different to me. You look at a picture and you instantly understand it, yet when you try to explain how a machine could do the same thing, you realize you have no idea. That gap fascinated me. It felt like one of the most fundamental questions of intelligence was sitting right there in front of everyone, hidden in something we take completely for granted.

So when other opportunities came up in different areas, some of them probably more established or more practical at the time, I just didn't feel that same pull. I remember thinking: if I'm going to spend my nights and weekends on research, it has to be something I'd want to think about even if nobody was asking me to. Doing research in an area I wasn't excited about felt like a waste of the one thing a student has a lot of, which is time and curiosity.

Looking back, it wasn't a very calculated decision. Back then, computer vision wasn't the obvious hot field it became after deep learning took off. It was more of a feeling that this was my problem. And I think that taught me something I still believe now: in research, taste and genuine interest matter a lot more than people admit. If you're working on something you don't really care about, you can be productive, but it's very hard to do something you're truly proud of.

r001.rationale: He says he was fascinated by the gap between understanding images and explaining how machines understand them, and that other fields lacked the same pull. This conveys wanting to understand computer vision more deeply as his reason for declining research elsewhere.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it came down to the fact that I'd already fallen in love with computer vision before I even knew what research really was. When I was an undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong, I'd gotten exposed to vision through some classes and a few projects, and there was something about it that just clicked for me. You're working with images, you can see what the algorithm is doing, you can see where it fails. That visual feedback loop felt very tangible compared to a lot of other areas.

So when there were opportunities to do research in other directions, things like databases or systems or more theoretical topics, I remember feeling like, if I spend my limited time on that, I'm not building toward the thing I actually care about. As an undergrad, your time is really scarce. You have maybe one or two summers, a thesis project, and you want those to add up to something.

I'll also admit there was a bit of stubbornness in it. Some people told me vision was crowded, or that I should diversify, and I think I reacted against that. I wanted to go deep rather than broad. Looking back, I don't think that's universally good advice. Plenty of great researchers wander around before they find their thing. But for me, having that clarity early meant I could start reading papers, learning the tools, and building intuition years before graduate school, and that compounding mattered a lot when I got to UCSD and later worked with Zhuowen Tu.

The one thing I'd caveat is that computer vision itself turned out to be much broader than I imagined at the time. So in a way I didn't really stay narrow. The field expanded underneath me.

r001.rationale: He says he wanted to go deep in computer vision and use his limited research time to build toward it, including reading papers and developing intuition—clearly conveying a desire to understand vision more deeply as the reason he declined work in other fields.

astra-6.text: I think “unwilling” is a little strong. I was already interested in computer vision, and I wanted to spend my time exploring that interest. As an undergraduate, you have limited time, so I felt it made sense to look for an opportunity in the area I was most curious about. It wasn’t a judgment that other areas were less valuable; it was about what motivated me.
